institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Santiago Bausili – Second-quarter Monetary Policy Report opening remarks
summary:
BCRA President Santiago Bausili said monthly inflation averaged 2.2% in the second quarter, down from 3.0% in the first. June headline inflation was 1.9%, and the BCRA's underlying index was 1.6%. He attributed the moderation partly to fading seasonal, administered-price and fuel pressures and argued that it also extended more broadly.

He said the second-quarter monetary policy orientation had remained unchanged. The President reported US$13.337 billion in foreign-exchange purchases through July 31 and described a recovery in demand for transactional money from May.
locator: Prepared opening remarks, sections III and IV on prices and monetary policy.

questions.question: Which categories drove the difference between headline and underlying June inflation?
questions.evidence: Bausili cites 1.9% headline and 1.6% on the Bank's underlying index. Compare the BCRA's underlying index weights with INDEC CPI contributions to assess how much of disinflation could persist as seasonal effects unwind.

questions.question: How should foreign-exchange purchases be reconciled with growth in peso demand?
questions.evidence: The remarks discuss reserve purchases and a recovery in transactional money demand. Reconcile BCRA reserve transactions, intervention and real deposit aggregates before attributing peso funding conditions to changes in liquidity.

questions.question: What data would test Bausili’s account of limited second-round effects?
questions.evidence: He attributes part of the disinflation to weaker pass-through and fading transitory influences. Compare time-stamped sector CPI, exchange rates and administered-price decisions to estimate the breadth and speed of pass-through.

coverageNote: Review covers the President’s published opening remarks.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Monthly Monetary Report – July 2026
summary:
In its July release series, the central bank reported that real seasonally adjusted transactional M2 rose 1.8% in July. Real time deposits fell 0.4%, and the broader M3 measure edged down. The report estimated real monetary base growth of 0.2%, with net foreign exchange purchases partly offset by operations involving the Treasury and secondary-market trades.

The report also described proposed charter amendments that would make preserving the value of money the central objective and bar new temporary advances to the Treasury. It presented these measures as elements of a draft. Separately, real seasonally adjusted peso credit to the private sector grew 1.2%, led by commercial loans.
locator: Official release, executive summary and linked report. Figures are from the August 7 publication vintage.

questions.question: Why did transactional money expand while the broader money measure fell?
questions.evidence: The report records rising transactional M2 and declining real time deposits. Break down the BCRA monetary tables by inflation adjustment, currency, demand deposits and time deposits to tell whether depositors are shortening maturity.

questions.question: How large were the offsetting effects of foreign exchange and Treasury transactions on the base?
questions.evidence: Net currency purchases supported the base while other operations partly offset them. Use the central bank's daily balance sheet and the Treasury cash timetable to distinguish potentially reversible operations before assessing peso funding.

questions.question: How would the draft restrictions change the balance-sheet channels through which the bank funds the Treasury?
questions.evidence: The report describes a proposed ban on temporary advances. Read the submitted bill and balance-sheet notes to establish which liabilities and asset transfers would be restricted and what changes would require enactment.

coverageNote: Review covers the executive summary. The draft charter provisions are identified separately from enacted rules.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Monthly Monetary Report – August 2026
summary:
The Bank reported unchanged real seasonally adjusted transactional M2 in August, with cash down 0.5% and sight deposits up 0.4%. The real monetary base increased 1.5%, which the Bank linked to higher reserve requirements generated by July demand deposits.

Real peso lending to the private sector fell 1% even as mortgage lending rose. Foreign-currency loans expanded by US$258 million to US$25.241 billion. The report discussed rules broadening eligible uses of US-dollar deposits under prudential criteria.
locator: Official release, executive summary and linked report. Figures are from the September 7 publication vintage.

questions.question: What is the lag between sight-deposit changes and required reserve demand?
questions.evidence: The report connects the August increase in the base to July demand deposits. Pair reserve computation dates and daily balances with deposit data to distinguish reserve-management effects from changes in underlying demand for money.

questions.question: What distinguishes continued mortgage growth from the broader contraction in real peso lending?
questions.evidence: Mortgage lending rose while total real peso loans fell. Compare loan originations, interest rates and maturity by product to assess whether mortgage lending can alter bank duration exposure.

questions.question: Which uses or borrowers explain expanding foreign-currency credit?
questions.evidence: The report describes a larger dollar loan book and changes to eligible uses of dollar deposits. Use BCRA monthly currency and borrower breakdowns and the text of the new rules to identify which balance sheets took on the additional dollar exposure.

coverageNote: Review covers the executive summary. Compare historical readings using a single data vintage before measuring changes.

institution: Banco Central de la República Argentina
title: Vladimir Werning – Address to the 47th IAEF Annual Convention
summary:
Vice President Vladimir Werning discussed Argentina's management of peso liquidity, foreign-exchange reserves and the credit cycle. He presented both cash and accrual-based estimates of net international reserves and said the difference reflected trade liabilities accumulated under earlier exchange restrictions.

Werning discussed the burden of credit costs and the differing reduction in rates for households and businesses since the 2025 election period. He framed the proposed BCRA charter reform as a means of formalizing limits on Treasury financing.
locator: BCRA event page published September 7 and linked prepared remarks, sections on foreign exchange, credit and structural reform. Delivered September 3.

questions.question: Which adjustments matter most when comparing cash and accrual measures of net international reserves?
questions.evidence: Werning distinguishes reserve measures by the treatment of trade liabilities. Reconcile trade credit and official reserves with contemporaneous balance-of-payments data to compare reserve coverage measures on the same basis.

questions.question: How does the divergence between household and business borrowing costs affect monetary transmission?
questions.evidence: The address discusses their unequal adjustment from the 2025 peak. Use new-lending rates, loan terms and delinquency by borrower type to see whether rate relief reached households and firms at different speeds.

questions.question: Which elements of the charter proposal could impose durable constraints on Treasury financing?
questions.evidence: Werning presents legal changes as a way to formalize recent policy practice. Compare provisions in the bill with existing law to evaluate which limits could constrain fiscal funding across future policy regimes.

coverageNote: Review covers the time-stamped event page and prepared speech dated September 3.

title: Copom reduces the Selic rate to 14.00%
summary:
The Copom reduced the Selic target by 25 basis points, from 14.25% to 14.00%, describing the resulting policy setting as still restrictive. Its reference projection placed inflation at 3.2% in the first quarter of 2028.

The committee described uncertainty around geopolitical effects on oil and possible El Niño effects. It flagged de-anchored expectations, persistent services inflation and a potentially weaker exchange rate among upside risks.
locator: Committee statement, inflation risk assessment and decision. Official comunicado 45.693 records the meeting decision.

questions.question: What makes the post-cut rate restrictive under alternative neutral-rate estimates?
questions.evidence: The committee reduced the nominal rate while calling the ensuing stance restrictive. Compare estimates of the real neutral rate with a maturity-matched expected real Selic path to assess how much restraint remains after the cut.

questions.question: Does services persistence reflect labour markets or broader pricing behaviour?
questions.evidence: Persistent services inflation appears in the upside risk discussion. Compare wage and vacancy indicators with price diffusion, regulated prices and commodity-sensitive services to test when the committee might see sustained disinflation.

questions.question: How sensitive is the Q1 2028 inflation projection to exchange rates and oil?
questions.evidence: The release discusses a potentially weaker currency and geopolitical commodity-price uncertainty. Use the Copom reference assumptions and alternative Brent and real paths to separate local inflation effects from the external drivers.

coverageNote: The official statement was reviewed from its published text as indexed. The linked site requires JavaScript to display the article in some environments.

title: Copom minutes – 280th meeting
summary:
The minutes give Copom's reference inflation projections of 5.1% for 2026, 3.8% for 2027 and 3.2% for the first quarter of 2028. The scenario used the Focus survey interest-rate path and a falling Brent futures path for the second half of 2026. The committee judged the risk balance to be skewed upward.

Members described continued low unemployment, slowing employment growth and real pay growth above productivity. They unanimously judged that de-anchored expectations required greater and longer monetary restriction than would otherwise be appropriate.
locator: Minutes of the August 4–5 meeting, risk scenario paragraphs 5–12 and Table 1. Release dated August 11.

questions.question: How sensitive are the reference projections to the assumed paths for crude and the Selic rate?
questions.evidence: The minutes set out both market-based assumptions. Use alternative oil and rate scenarios with the committee's published inflation model to test forecasts that could alter the expected Selic path.

questions.question: To what extent could real wage growth above productivity sustain services inflation?
questions.evidence: The labour section compares real wage growth and productivity. Compare official wage, productivity and services inflation indicators at comparable frequencies before treating wage growth as a forward inflation signal.

questions.question: What evidence would convince the committee that expectations are re-anchoring?
questions.evidence: Members identify persistent de-anchoring as requiring longer and greater restriction. Compare the Focus distribution with indexed-bond measures adjusted for liquidity and risk premia to test whether anchoring extends beyond surveys.

title: Copom reduces the Selic rate to 13.75%
summary:
The Copom reduced the Selic target by 25 basis points to 13.75%. It described a gradual moderation concentrated in more cyclical activities, with a resilient economy and a tight labour market. Focus survey inflation expectations were 4.9% for 2026 and 4.3% for 2027.

The communication emphasized uncertainty in the external environment and the interaction of domestic fiscal conditions with inflation and monetary conditions.
locator: Committee statement, economic backdrop, Focus expectations and decision. Official comunicado 45.963 records the meeting decision.

questions.question: How uneven is the slowdown across cyclical and less rate-sensitive industries?
questions.evidence: The committee described moderation concentrated in cyclical sectors. Compare output and hiring data in rate-sensitive sectors and slower-moving services to assess the breadth of policy transmission.

questions.question: How far above target were private inflation expectations at comparable horizons?
questions.evidence: The decision identifies the 2026 and 2027 Focus survey expectations. Compare the Focus distribution and inflation compensation at the same horizons to determine whether the survey path represents wider market pricing.

questions.question: How can local funding conditions distinguish external rate pressure from domestic fiscal effects?
questions.evidence: The committee discusses external and domestic fiscal influences on financial conditions. Use time-stamped BRL rates and sovereign spreads around independent fiscal and external news to test their relative contribution to domestic duration risk.

coverageNote: The official statement was reviewed from its published text as indexed. The linked site requires JavaScript to display the article in some environments.

title: Copom minutes – 281st meeting
summary:
The September minutes describe accumulating evidence of restrictive policy reaching economic activity. Copom distinguished the initial effect of supply shocks from possible second-round effects and considered inflation risks tilted up. The members present listed in the minutes all supported reducing the Selic target to 13.75%.

Copom's reference projections were 5.2% for 2026, 3.9% for 2027 and 3.2% in the first quarter of 2028. The minutes present these projections separately from private expectations.
locator: Minutes, sections B–D, paragraphs 14–20 and Table 1. September 15–16 meeting, release dated September 22.

questions.question: Which data best capture the lagged response to restrictive policy?
questions.evidence: The minutes say evidence of transmission to activity was accumulating. Compare consumer-credit originations and rate-sensitive investment across several preceding quarters to assess when policy may affect underlying inflation.

questions.question: Where could energy or commodity prices spread into persistent underlying inflation?
questions.evidence: Copom distinguishes direct supply effects from possible second-round effects. Use official price microdata and the bank's oil pass-through work to measure dissemination into services and wages that matter for the policy horizon.

questions.question: What moved the near-term forecast higher while the policy-horizon estimate held?
questions.evidence: The September forecast table can be compared with the August minutes. Read the September Monetary Policy Report's forecast decomposition to identify offsets that could reverse with a change in oil, expectations or slack.

title: Monetary Policy Report – September 2026
summary:
The Bank lowered its 2026 GDP growth forecast from 2.0% to 1.8% and projected 1.4% in 2027. Second-quarter GDP rose 0.5% from the previous quarter after 1.1% in the first quarter. Household consumption fell and cyclical sectors slowed, while the labour market remained strong.

Annual headline inflation fell from 4.72% in May to 4.22% in August. The report said services inflation remained elevated. The reference projection for the first quarter of 2028 remained 3.2%, with a generally higher inflation path and a projected 5.2% at the end of 2026.
locator: Report executive summary, pp. 5–6, output, inflation and reference scenario. BCB publication date September 24.

questions.question: What portion of the GDP downgrade stems from household spending versus other cyclical components?
questions.evidence: The Bank cites Q2 composition and weak early Q3 indicators. Compare the Bank's sector forecasts with national accounts and early Q3 consumption to estimate the weight of rate-sensitive domestic demand.

questions.question: Which services components remain elevated despite slowing overall prices?
questions.evidence: The report contrasts easing headline inflation with services persistence. Compare CPI subindexes with wages and service activity to test which components could slow the return toward the target.

questions.question: What offset higher expected inflation and a larger output gap at the forecast horizon?
questions.evidence: The report identifies recent inflation surprises and a near-term reversal in oil prices as downward offsets. Use the report's forecast decomposition and alternative scenarios to estimate which offsets would still hold if oil prices and expectations moved together.

coverageNote: Review covers the official executive summary.

title: Trial of Government of Canada securities settlement fail fees
summary:
The Collateral Infrastructure and Market Practices Advisory Group and the Canadian Depository for Securities announced a September 8 start for the first stage of a fee trial on settlement fails in Government of Canada bonds and treasury bills. The stage was scheduled to last at least 18 months.

The trial calculates indicative fees and supplies fail statistics and participant reports. A subsequent decision by the Canadian Fixed-Income Forum would be needed to activate payments.
locator: Bank-hosted market notice, trial mechanics and decision authority.

questions.question: Which issues or tenors account for the most persistent fails during the trial?
questions.evidence: The first stage makes statistics available on Government of Canada bond and bill fails. Use CDS fail counts and auction issue identifiers to test whether settlement risk clusters in collateral relevant to pricing or hedging.

questions.question: Do participants change settlement behaviour when they receive indicative invoices?
questions.evidence: The notice specifies that reports and indicative fees are available during the first stage. Compare failures and indicative invoice exposure around implementation while accounting for seasonal settlement patterns and issuance.

questions.question: How would a decision to activate payments affect repo spreads for scarce collateral?
questions.evidence: The forum retained authority for any subsequent decision on actual payments. Compare security-level repo quotes and fails before and after any future activation to assess the prospective cost of financing short positions.

coverageNote: Joint market infrastructure notice hosted by the Bank. The notice describes trial design.

title: Quarterly Financial Report – Second Quarter 2026
summary:
The Bank reported second-quarter net income of C$298 million and first-half net income of C$479 million. It retained the earnings to reduce its accumulated deficit. Higher term and overnight repo activity supported year-over-year interest revenue despite lower interest generated by investments.

During the first half the Bank continued purchases through term and overnight repos and Government of Canada treasury bills. The report presented these operations in its account of assets and deposit balances.
locator: Management overview, financial position and financial results. Fiscal data to June 30; the publication is dated August 19.

questions.question: How did the composition of the Bank's short-term assets change as settlement balances declined?
questions.evidence: The financial-position discussion connects the change in deposits with investments and repos. Compare the detailed statements and the Bank's settlement-balance series to assess the maturity mix and the potential implications for funding-market liquidity.

questions.question: How much of the net-income improvement came from higher repo volumes?
questions.evidence: The income discussion attributes higher interest revenue in part to repos. Reconcile repo volumes, rates and investment maturities in the quarterly notes to separate effects of earning assets from interest expense.

questions.question: How persistent could the accumulated deficit be under different funding costs?
questions.evidence: The Bank retained net income to reduce that deficit. Use the report's balance-sheet notes and maturity schedule to test net-income scenarios and the point at which remittances could resume.

coverageNote: Review covers management commentary and financial highlights. The underlying statements are unaudited.

title: Bank of Canada maintains policy rate at 2¼%
summary:
The Bank held the overnight target at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.50% and the deposit rate at 2.20%. It described a broad second-quarter recovery, with real GDP rising at a 3.3% annualized rate. The July unemployment rate had improved to 6.4%, with labour demand still subdued.

Governing Council described tariffs as a downside risk to growth and higher oil and refining margins as upside risks to prices. Headline inflation was near 3%, inflation excluding gasoline was 2.2% in July and core measures were close to 2%. The Bank reported limited pass-through to other prices at the time.
locator: Policy-rate announcement, Canadian activity and inflation paragraphs, and final guidance.

questions.question: Which sectors account for the rebound, and where does tariff exposure still weigh on activity?
questions.evidence: The release pairs a second-quarter recovery with tariff-related growth risks. Use industry GDP, export volumes and business investment to test whether the recovery extends beyond temporary factors.

questions.question: Does gasoline inflation subsequently spill into broader prices?
questions.evidence: Inflation excluding gasoline was 2.2% and the Bank described limited pass-through. Compare ex-energy price diffusion, firm pricing intentions and wage growth before revising the expected rate path for higher headline CPI.

questions.question: What was priced before the announcement for the date and path of the overnight target?
questions.evidence: The unchanged rate and conditional guidance provide a comparison point for an independently measured expectations series. Use Bank release timestamps and matched CORRA futures or swaps to estimate the surprise and separate it from earlier moves in the Canadian dollar and longer yields.

title: Summary of Governing Council deliberations – September 2, 2026
summary:
Governing Council held the policy rate at 2.25%, judging growth and inflation broadly in line with the July forecast. Members discussed whether weakness linked to new US tariffs would absorb the impact of higher energy prices. Excess supply and a soft labour market could keep price pressures contained.

Members agreed that spillovers from higher energy prices to other CPI components could warrant a policy response. They said the durability of the recovery and the extent of pass-through would inform the inflation forecast and its associated risks.
locator: Bank’s deliberations, discussion of the balance of risks and Policy decision. September 2 decision, minutes published September 16.

questions.question: What indicators would establish broader energy-price pass-through?
questions.evidence: Members said material spillover to other prices could warrant a response. Use CPI microdata and supplier-cost surveys to establish whether pass-through has spread enough to affect the near-term rate path.

questions.question: How is tariff-induced uncertainty affecting the durability of the recovery?
questions.evidence: Members linked tariffs and confidence to uncertainty about the recovery. Compare industrial order books and business expectations in more and less exposed sectors before revising the likely duration of slack.

questions.question: Which measures of excess supply explain differences in inflation risk assessments?
questions.evidence: The minutes discuss spare capacity and a soft labour market as possible offsets to energy pressure. Compare the Bank's slack measures with capacity utilization and job vacancies to test whether alternative estimates change the projected inflation response.

title: Tiff Macklem – Navigating uncertainty and adapting to change
summary:
Governor Tiff Macklem described new US tariffs and elevated energy prices as distinct risks to growth and inflation. He expected relatively contained direct aggregate effects from the latest tariffs because the affected products made up about 5% of Canadian goods exports to the United States, but said broader uncertainty could delay hiring and investment.

He said the Bank would track the persistence of energy costs, their pass-through to goods and services, and whether slack weakened inflation pressure. Macklem said the Bank planned to use its new forecasting model, Prima, as the primary model for the October Monetary Policy Report.
locator: Prepared speech, New challenges ahead and How the Bank is thinking about it.

questions.question: How are investment and hiring responding outside the sectors directly affected by tariffs?
questions.evidence: Macklem distinguishes limited direct tariff exposure from broader effects of uncertainty. Match trade exposure to Canadian investment intentions and job postings to assess whether second-round demand effects exceed the direct export exposure.

questions.question: What would indicate second-round effects of higher energy costs?
questions.evidence: He discusses businesses passing costs on and households changing longer-term expectations. Compare sector selling prices, firm pricing intentions and long-term expectations to distinguish cost recovery from a broad inflation process.

questions.question: How does Prima handle temporary and persistent inflation scenarios?
questions.evidence: Macklem says distinguishing those forces is one purpose of the model. Use the Bank's model documentation and published alternative scenarios to assess how persistence assumptions change the forecast that guides decisions.

coverageNote: Review covers the published prepared speech.

title: Monetary Policy Report – July 2026
summary:
The technical staff reported June headline inflation of 6.1%, up from 5.6% in March, and June inflation excluding food and regulated prices of 6.0%. It described pressure from labour and production costs, firm household and public spending, and agricultural disruptions. Peso appreciation partly tempered price pressure.

The staff projected headline inflation of 6.9% at year-end 2026 and 4.3% at year-end 2027, against the 3% target. It also described expansion in consumption and capital-equipment investment. Growth was 2.2% year over year in the first quarter. The staff projected 2.5% growth for 2026 and 1.9% for 2027, with a weaker impulse from some recent demand drivers.
locator: Official release page, inflation outlook and activity overview. July edition published August 4.

questions.question: Which services are most responsive to higher labour costs?
questions.evidence: The report cites labour costs in discussing persistent inflation. Use sector CPI and wage series across services to test which prices could keep inflation high after agricultural disruptions fade.

questions.question: How do household and public spending contribute to the inflation path separately?
questions.evidence: The staff describes both sources of firm demand. Reconcile national accounts demand components and official fiscal execution data before attributing the projected inflation path to private consumption or fiscal support.

questions.question: What exchange-rate pass-through assumptions underpin the return toward target?
questions.evidence: The report cites recent peso appreciation as a partial offset and forecasts lower year-end inflation in 2027. Read the report's model and exchange-rate sensitivity assumptions to identify which peso trajectories materially alter the return toward target.

coverageNote: Review covers the published landing-page overview and figures.

title: Board minutes – Policy rate held at 12.00%
summary:
The minutes record four votes to maintain the 12.00% policy rate and three for a 50-basis-point increase. The majority supported a pause to assess earlier tightening. Some members pointed to stable June core inflation and the influence of prices affected by weather and international shocks.

The directors favouring an increase emphasized the risk of broader inflation from El Niño, the limited change in the ex-ante real policy stance relative to a year earlier, and the risks of delaying further tightening. The minutes cited July analyst expectations of 6.6% for December 2026 and 5.0% for December 2027.
locator: Official minutes, opening vote and majority and minority discussion. Published August 5 for the July decision.

questions.question: Which indicators are most informative about the lagged impact of prior rate increases?
questions.evidence: The majority paused to assess transmission from previous increases. Compare monthly credit, lending rates and activity with earlier policy moves to see whether the majority's rationale holds as the data arrive.

questions.question: How does the neutral-rate estimate change the real-rate-gap comparison?
questions.evidence: Supporters of a larger increase cited a broadly similar ex-ante real policy stance to a year earlier. Use the Bank's real neutral-rate research and like-for-like inflation expectations to see how assumptions affect conclusions about existing restriction.

questions.question: Which indicators distinguish a weather-driven relative-price change from general inflation?
questions.evidence: The two sides discussed supply-driven inflation and the possibility that it spreads. Use price diffusion, weather monitoring and inflation expectations to distinguish a sectoral shock from a shift that could affect the nominal policy path.

title: The regional effects of monetary policy in Colombia
summary:
Using Colombian city and department observations from 2008 to 2025, Cristian David González-Téllez and Juan Camilo Laborde-Vera report that a rate increase reduces inflation, activity and employment by different amounts across regions. Jointly larger responses in prices and output point to differences in local demand sensitivity in the authors’ interpretation.

The paper identifies surprises using dealer forecasts, narrative evidence and market moves around decisions. It reports larger activity declines in mining regions and greater contractions across the studied outcomes in regions with above-trend bank credit, higher trade integration or more informal employment.
locator: Working-paper landing page, approach, contribution and results. Direct page date is September 21.

questions.question: Which regional results are strongest across the three monetary shock measures?
questions.evidence: The authors use survey, narrative and high-frequency market identification. Read the paper's regional impulse responses and confidence intervals for each measure to assess how much precision regional forecasts can claim.

questions.question: Can credit depth and sector composition separately explain regional transmission?
questions.evidence: The study reports response differences associated with regional credit and industrial mix. Check controls and alternative model specifications before using the estimates to rank regional credit risk.

questions.question: How might a region's trade integration change the relevance of its exchange-rate channel?
questions.evidence: Greater trade integration is associated with larger estimated responses. Use sector trade shares and regional price responses to test whether openness proxies for currency sensitivity or another part of the transmission.

coverageNote: Review covers the official research summary. The findings are the authors’ provisional research, with no policy decision implied.

title: Board raises the monetary policy interest rate to 12.25%
summary:
Four directors voted to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points to 12.25%, two voted to hold and one preferred a 50-basis-point increase. August headline inflation was 6.2%, services inflation 7.2%, and inflation excluding food and regulated prices 6.1%. Analyst expectations for year-end 2026 increased to 6.8%, while the two-year measure eased to 4%.

Second-quarter GDP was 3.4% above a year earlier, while the July activity indicator grew 1.1%. The Board cited risks from El Niño, earthquake effects and fiscal measures, and noted that government-bond-implied inflation expectations exceeded the 3% target.
locator: Official release, vote paragraph, inflation and activity points, and outlook.

questions.question: What explains the gap between near-term and two-year expectations?
questions.evidence: Year-end analyst expectations rose, while the two-year measure fell. Compare survey distributions with government-bond inflation compensation after allowing for liquidity to assess which part of the curve reflects persistent inflation risk.

questions.question: How should services inflation be weighted relative to slowing activity?
questions.evidence: Services inflation was 7.2% and the July activity indicator grew more slowly than second-quarter GDP. Use disaggregated CPI and the activity indicators available at release to test whether service pressure or wider demand weakness better predicts core momentum.

questions.question: Which inflation or demand outcomes would shift members on either side of the 25-basis-point majority?
questions.evidence: The published vote shows hold and larger-increase alternatives. Study subsequent officially published minutes as they become available and track the inflation or demand measures each group cites in explaining its vote.

title: Monetary policy announcement – August 6, 2026
summary:
The Governing Board unanimously held the overnight interbank target at 6.50%. From the first half of June to the first half of July, annual headline inflation declined from 3.55% to 3.10% and core inflation fell from 4.12% to 3.95%. The Bank projected a more gradual disinflation path and convergence to 3% in the fourth quarter of 2027, with inflation risks still skewed upward.

The Bank reported a second-quarter rebound after a first-quarter contraction. It assessed the economy as still having slack and viewed growth risks as tilted down.
locator: Official statement pp. 1–2, activity, forecast table, risk balance and decision.

questions.question: How much of June-to-July disinflation reflected temporary non-core price moves?
questions.evidence: Headline inflation fell more than core between the stated fortnightly observations. Compare fortnightly CPI contributions and monthly seasonal patterns to test how much disinflation can persist.

questions.question: Which core components account for slower expected convergence?
questions.evidence: The decision retained an upside-skewed risk balance and projected convergence in Q4 2027. Use forecasts and actual services and merchandise inflation to distinguish slower trend disinflation from volatile monthly releases.

questions.question: How did the changes in the peso and local yields discussed by the Bank predate the release?
questions.evidence: The announcement compares prevailing market conditions with the preceding policy decision. Compare independently time-stamped TIIE swaps and peso quotes around the publication before attributing any move to the decision.

title: Governing Board minutes – August 6 monetary policy decision
summary:
All five voting members supported keeping the overnight interbank rate at 6.50%. The account distinguishes policy views within that vote. One member discussed a neutral stance, noted uncertainty about potential GDP and argued that slack was secondary for choosing the stance during potential supply shocks. Another emphasized that transmission was still helping disinflation and that the exchange rate suggested room to absorb changes in conditions abroad.

A separate argument for a hold was that it addressed persistent inflation components and external risks while leaving flexibility to reassess easing inflation pressure. The individual views are presented without identifying speakers in the discussion section.
locator: Minutes, monetary-policy discussion and Votación, official printed pp. 11–14. Decision August 6, minutes released August 20.

questions.question: How sensitive are conclusions about slack to potential-output revisions?
questions.evidence: A member noted that a lower estimate of potential GDP would imply a smaller gap. Compare the activity data available to the Board and different real-time potential-output estimates before relying on slack as a rate catalyst.

questions.question: What would establish that monetary transmission is continuing rather than fading?
questions.evidence: A member linked disinflation to ongoing transmission. Compare contemporary credit conditions, core components and the timing of prior rate changes to test how demand is responding.

questions.question: How much protection could the exchange rate offer against an external tightening shock?
questions.evidence: A member cited the exchange rate as evidence of a buffer. Examine timestamped peso, overnight-indexed swap and US-rate data around prior external surprises, controlling for simultaneous Mexican releases.

coverageNote: Review covers the policy discussion and voting section, excluding the full statistical annex.

title: Quarterly Report – April to June 2026
summary:
Banco de México raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast from 1.1% to 1.5% and reduced the 2027 forecast from 2.1% to 2.0%. It still estimated a negative output gap throughout its forecast. The report characterized the growth risk balance as tilted down amid uncertainty around trade negotiations and geopolitical developments.

The report also reviewed headline and core inflation forecasts, and kept its projection of convergence to the 3% target in the fourth quarter of 2027. The revised path reflected higher core inflation over much of the horizon and higher non-core inflation in the first three quarters of 2027 relative to the prior report.
locator: Executive summary PDF, pp. 5–8, GDP growth Table 1, output-gap chart and inflation forecasts.

questions.question: What explains the upward 2026 GDP revision and slight downward 2027 revision?
questions.evidence: Table 1 compares both estimates with the previous quarterly report. Compare the growth fan chart, revised quarterly history and sector assumptions to distinguish a mechanical carryover from better underlying momentum.

questions.question: Which real-time data could narrow uncertainty about a negative output gap?
questions.evidence: The Bank projects a negative gap and notes the uncertainty of an unobserved measure. Use contemporaneous labour-market and capacity indicators with alternative potential-output estimates to test how sensitive the rate outlook is to the gap.

questions.question: How do near-term headline revisions change the inflation profile without changing the eventual objective?
questions.evidence: The inflation table retains the August 6 forecast, which revised the shape of headline and core inflation relative to the prior quarterly report. Compare the forecast table by quarter and component to identify which pressures could change rate expectations.

coverageNote: Review covers the Bank’s published executive summary.

title: August 2026 survey of private-sector economic expectations
summary:
The median private-sector forecast for December 2026 headline inflation moved from 4.00% in July to 3.90% in August. The core median moved from 4.00% to 3.99%, and median 2026 GDP growth rose from 1.20% to 1.30%. The median forecasts for year-end interbank rates held at 6.50% for 2026 and 2027.

The median year-end 2026 exchange-rate estimate fell from 17.88 to 17.50 pesos per US dollar. The Bank collected responses between August 18 and August 26.
locator: Private-sector survey, front-page overview and Table 1. August fieldwork, release dated September 1.

questions.question: What drove the larger change in headline than core expectations?
questions.evidence: Table 1 records a 0.10-point move in the headline median and a 0.01-point move in core. Check distributions and component forecasts against available non-core price releases to determine whether the headline revision is broad or reflects a few respondents.

questions.question: How much information does the unchanged policy-rate median conceal about the distribution?
questions.evidence: Year-end rate medians remained 6.50% for both years. Review the response distribution and contemporaneous swaps to see whether stable medians mask more weight on a change in the rate outlook.

questions.question: How do differences in survey and market dates affect comparisons of expected peso levels?
questions.evidence: The report gives a fieldwork window and a year-end median exchange-rate forecast. Match dealer forecasts to the August survey window and separate spot from forwards when interpreting the expected currency change.

coverageNote: Review covers the overview and Table 1. The forecasts are those of survey respondents.

title: Monetary policy announcement – September 24, 2026
summary:
The Governing Board unanimously kept the overnight interbank target at 6.50%. From the first half of July to the first half of September, annual headline inflation rose from 3.10% to 3.42%, driven by non-core inflation, while core fell from 3.95% to 3.79%. The Bank lowered its near-term headline forecast, modestly lifted its third- and fourth-quarter 2026 core forecasts, and retained fourth-quarter 2027 convergence to 3%.

The Board reported slowing activity and slack. The announcement noted a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve increase and described differences in domestic transmission relevant to Mexico's policy decision.
locator: Official statement pp. 1–2, activity, inflation forecast table and final paragraphs.

questions.question: Which price components explain the different revisions to headline and core forecasts?
questions.evidence: The Bank lowered the near-term headline path while lifting two near-term core forecasts. Compare the statement's vintage tables with INEGI CPI contributions to identify which assumptions could alter the expected pace of easing.

questions.question: How might domestic slack mediate pass-through from external rates?
questions.evidence: The Board reported slack and emphasized differences in monetary transmission. Compare local lending rates, the peso and measures of credit and utilization after external moves to see whether changes in US rates reach domestic inflation.

questions.question: How does the decision compare with the market's pre-release probability of a rate change?
questions.evidence: The Board voted unanimously for an unchanged rate after discussing external tightening. Compare TIIE pricing just before the published time with like-for-like rates afterward and identify other releases within the same window.

title: August 2026 monetary program – Reference rate maintained at 4.25%
summary:
The central bank announced that its board maintained the monetary-policy reference rate at 4.25% in the August program. The Bank's separate official daily series displays the level around the August 13 meeting.

The central bank's short public announcement confirms the action. A full review of the decision rationale and projections would require the detailed program materials.
locator: Central bank's decision-day post and its daily reference-rate series PD12301MD.

questions.question: What did the local-currency yield curve price before the release for August and the next meeting?
questions.evidence: The BCRP confirms the unchanged 4.25% benchmark. Compare the release time with local rates or quotes on both sides of the announcement so pre-release expectations can be distinguished from the policy action.

questions.question: Which inflation or activity inputs did the full statement identify as decisive?
questions.evidence: The public post confirms the choice of rate and points to the August program. Read the official monetary-program presentation and dated underlying CPI, expectations and activity inputs to see which arguments could shape the subsequent rate path.

questions.question: How does the August wording compare with September once both statements are available?
questions.evidence: The headline confirms the August policy action but gives limited rationale. Use the August release as the baseline and compare its risk paragraph with September's official publication to distinguish changing data from changing guidance.

coverageNote: Based on the official announcement and rate series. The policy PDF was inaccessible during review.

title: July 2026 liquidity and credit statistics – Private-sector credit
summary:
The central bank reported that total private-sector credit rose 9.4% from a year earlier and 1.3% from the preceding month in July. The two growth rates compare the outstanding aggregate over different horizons.

The bank's accompanying institutional post identifies the July liquidity and credit research note. The headline tally gives a reference point for credit conditions as of its August publication.
locator: Bank’s dated chart release on private-sector credit and official announcement for the July liquidity and credit edition.

questions.question: How broad was July credit growth across households and firms?
questions.evidence: The chart shows a positive aggregate. To see whether it reflects stronger general credit demand, compare sectoral balances and loans by purpose in the July BCRP statistical tables.

questions.question: How much of the change reflects exchange-rate valuation?
questions.evidence: Total credit is the subject of the official chart. Compare original-currency figures and exchange-rate-adjusted aggregates before inferring lending momentum.

questions.question: What did new lending volumes imply about monetary transmission?
questions.evidence: The chart measures outstanding balances. Bank lending reports on originations, repayments and repricing could establish how credit flows changed.

coverageNote: The primary source reviewed is BCRP’s August 28 chart release. The underlying research-note link was inaccessible.

institution: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú
title: September 2026 monetary program – Reference rate maintained at 4.25%
summary:
The Bank announced that it held the reference rate at 4.25%. In the Bank's accompanying video, it reported that August annual inflation rose from 4.1% to 4.4%, influenced by the comparison base, while inflation excluding food and energy declined from 4.6% to 4.5%. The bank reported 12-month inflation expectations of 3.1% and 24-month expectations of 2.5%.

The Bank described energy and transport as important contributors and reported underlying inflation of 1.8% excluding transport. It expected headline and underlying inflation to return to the target range and settle around 2% over its forecast horizon as the supply shocks fade. It cited weather and geopolitical risks and described activity indicators as strong.
locator: Decision-day announcement and official September monetary-program video transcript, especially the inflation and outlook segments.

questions.question: How much of the August rise can be decomposed into base effects and subsequent price momentum?
questions.evidence: The Bank highlighted the comparison base while headline inflation increased. Reconstruct prior-year monthly contributions and the current seasonally adjusted CPI to estimate momentum relevant to the next policy decision.

questions.question: How persistent are the transport pressures embedded in underlying inflation?
questions.evidence: The Bank described energy and transport as key contributors. Use BCRP transport and ex-transport underlying measures with fuel-price series to test how durable the contribution may be.

questions.question: Why were 12-month expectations above two-year expectations?
questions.evidence: The Bank reported 3.1% at 12 months and 2.5% at 24 months. Compare response distributions at matching horizons and other official expectations series to gauge whether the rise reflects temporary shocks or broader concern.

coverageNote: Based on the official decision announcement and accompanying video transcript. The detailed decision PDF was inaccessible during review.

institution: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú
title: August 2026 liquidity and credit statistics – Private-sector credit in soles
summary:
The Bank reported that the outstanding stock of private-sector credit denominated in soles rose 9.1% from a year earlier and 1.6% from July. The Bank's release describes a currency-specific aggregate for August.

The Bank's other highlights for the August edition include the same 1.6% monthly increase for total private-sector credit and a 10.3% annual increase in that broader measure. The different coverage matters when comparing the annual rates.
locator: Bank’s chart release for sol-denominated credit and the adjacent official total-credit highlight in the August liquidity and credit release.

questions.question: What explains the gap between local-currency and total annual credit growth?
questions.evidence: The official highlights report 9.1% in soles and 10.3% overall. Compare the original-currency balance sheets and methodology to separate actual dollar credit expansion from valuation.

questions.question: How widespread was growth in sol credit across borrower types?
questions.evidence: The chart is a private-sector aggregate. Check BCRP loan balances by recipient and purpose, plus supervisory delinquency figures if assessing bank credit risk.

questions.question: Are household and corporate borrowing costs consistent with the rise in balances?
questions.evidence: The chart reports balances over time. Compare rates on new loans and sector-level loan flows for evidence of pass-through from the policy rate.

coverageNote: Review covers BCRP's published highlights on local-currency and total lending. The underlying research-note link was inaccessible.
